questions.stem: A 36 year old man has a haemoglobin of 189 g/L on a blood test after returning from 18 months working at a mine 4,000 m up in the Andes. He feels well. His oxygen saturation is 92% breathing air. Investigations: white cell count 6.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 260 ×10⁹/L (150–400) and serum erythropoietin raised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic hypoxia at high altitude drives a raised EPO, with normal white cells and platelets: secondary polycythaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hypoxia from altitude, isolated high Hb, raised EPO.

elim: White cell count is normal.
His platelet count is normal.
Would usually raise white cells and platelets too, with a low erythropoietin.
Due to low plasma volume from dehydration or diuretics; EPO would not be raised.

steps.x: **E. Secondary polycythaemia.** Raised EPO + normal WCC and platelets + hypoxia = secondary polycythaemia.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has 2 months of painless visible haematuria and a dull right loin ache. He has lost 4 kg. His oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air and his chest is clear. Investigations: haemoglobin 196 g/L (130–180), normal white cells and platelets, raised serum erythropoietin and a negative JAK2 mutation screen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his raised haemoglobin?
questions.e: An EPO-producing tumour such as renal cell carcinoma causes secondary polycythaemia with raised EPO and normal oxygen saturation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Raised EPO without hypoxia, plus haematuria and loin pain.

elim: His saturation is normal and his chest is clear.
Would not raise erythropoietin.
No snoring or daytime sleepiness, and no hypoxia.
JAK2 is negative and EPO is raised.

steps.x: **E. Renal cell carcinoma.** High EPO with normal saturation: look for an EPO-secreting tumour (renal).

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has uncorrected congenital heart disease with a ventricular septal defect and Eisenmenger syndrome. She has finger clubbing and central cyanosis. Her oxygen saturation is 81% breathing air. Her haemoglobin is 212 g/L (115–165), with normal white cells and platelets.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her raised haemoglobin?
questions.e: Cyanotic heart disease causes chronic hypoxia, raising EPO and red cell mass: secondary polycythaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Chronic hypoxia from a right-to-left shunt.

elim: Platelets are normal.
Does not raise haemoglobin.
Cyanotic heart disease gives an obvious hypoxic drive; other lines are normal.
She has a true rise driven by hypoxia, not low plasma volume.

steps.x: **E. Secondary polycythaemia.** Cyanotic heart disease, COPD, OSA, altitude: secondary polycythaemia (EPO high).

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with polycythaemia vera wakes with a hot, red, extremely painful right big toe. He cannot bear the bedsheet touching it. He has had venesection every 6 weeks. His temperature is 37.6°C. His serum urate is 0.58 mmol/L (0.20–0.43).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: High red cell turnover in PV raises urate, so gout is a recognised complication.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
PV plus acute first MTP joint inflammation and raised urate.

elim: Spreading skin infection rather than a single acutely inflamed joint with high urate.
Burning, red extremities triggered by heat, not one swollen joint.
Gradual pain and stiffness, not acute severe inflammation.
Usually affects the knee, with calcium pyrophosphate, not high urate.

steps.x: **C. Gout.** PV complications include gout from high cell turnover.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has had polycythaemia vera for 18 years. Over 6 weeks she has become increasingly lethargic and breathless, with bruising. Investigations: haemoglobin 84 g/L (115–165), white cell count 46 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) and platelets 32 ×10⁹/L (150–400). Her blood film shows 30% blasts.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Long-standing PV can rarely transform to AML: low Hb and platelets, high white count with blasts, and rising lethargy.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Long-standing PV now with marrow failure and ≥20% blasts.

elim: Causes cytopenias but not a high white count with blasts.
Causes microcytic anaemia, not blasts or a high white count.
Would show teardrop cells and a big spleen; 30% blasts means acute leukaemia.
Her haemoglobin is now low.

steps.x: **E. Transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia.** PV late complications: myelofibrosis (spent phase) or, rarely, AML.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has 4 months of headaches, tinnitus and itching after a hot bath. He has never smoked and has no lung disease. His oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air. Investigations: haemoglobin 198 g/L (130–180), white cell count 12.6 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) and platelets 560 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Polycythaemia vera causes a plethoric, ruddy face, along with aquagenic pruritus and splenomegaly.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Aquagenic itch and all three lines raised without hypoxia: PV.

elim: He is not hypoxic.
Suggests chronic lung disease, cyanotic heart disease or lung cancer.
A sign of iron deficiency, not of a raised haemoglobin.
A sign of chronic liver disease.

steps.x: **D. Plethoric facies.** PV signs: facial plethora, splenomegaly, erythromelalgia; symptom: aquagenic pruritus.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has 3 months of dizziness, ringing in her ears, aching muscles and episodes of blurred vision. She feels tired all the time. She has never smoked. Her oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air. Investigations: haemoglobin 188 g/L (115–165), white cell count 13.0 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 610 ×10⁹/L (150–400) and serum erythropoietin low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Raised Hb with raised white cells and platelets and a low EPO is polycythaemia vera, a JAK2 myeloproliferative disorder.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hyperviscosity symptoms, all lines raised, low EPO, no hypoxia.

elim: Would show a much higher white count and does not raise haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin would be normal.
Causes anaemia, not a raised haemoglobin.
EPO would be raised and white cells and platelets normal.

steps.x: **C. Polycythaemia vera.** Low EPO + raised Hb, WCC and platelets = PV.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man with polycythaemia vera has stopped attending venesection. He has 40 minutes of crushing central chest pain radiating to his jaw. His pulse rate is 56 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. His haematocrit is 0.61 (0.40–0.52). ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG on arrival
visual.caption: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL: inferior STEMI.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: PV raises blood viscosity, predisposing to arterial thrombosis such as MI; ST elevation in II, III and aVF is an inferior STEMI.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Uncontrolled PV with typical ischaemic pain.

elim: Causes widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation without reciprocal change, and pleuritic pain.
Tearing pain radiating to the back.
Causes pleuritic pain and breathlessness, usually with sinus tachycardia.
Pain lasts minutes on exertion, without ST elevation.

steps.x: **A. Acute inferior myocardial infarction.** PV thrombotic complications: MI, stroke, DVT, PE, Budd-Chiari.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has a haemoglobin of 186 g/L (130–180) found on a routine blood test. He smokes 40 cigarettes a day. He has no breathlessness, cough or snoring, and spirometry is normal. His carboxyhaemoglobin level is 9%. White cells and platelets are normal and his JAK2 screen is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his raised haemoglobin?
questions.e: Heavy smoking raises carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing oxygen delivery and raising EPO: a cause of secondary polycythaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Heavy smoker with a high carboxyhaemoglobin and no lung disease.

elim: No history of steroid use.
Spirometry is normal.
No snoring or daytime sleepiness.
JAK2 is negative and other cell lines are normal.

steps.x: **C. Cigarette smoking.** Smoking is a common cause of secondary polycythaemia.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with severe COPD and secondary polycythaemia has a haematocrit of 0.59 (0.40–0.52). He suddenly loses the ability to speak and has weakness of his right arm. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and regular, BP 158/90 mmHg and capillary glucose 6.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Secondary polycythaemia carries the same thrombotic risks as PV, including ischaemic stroke.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: suddenly loses the ability to speak
steps.x: High haematocrit and a sudden focal neurological deficit.

elim: Facial weakness only, without arm weakness or loss of speech.
Causes drowsiness and flap, not sudden focal deficits.
His glucose is normal.
Follows a seizure, which has not happened.

steps.x: **D. Ischaemic stroke.** Secondary polycythaemia: stroke, MI, DVT/PE risk too.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has 2 months of headaches and a red complexion. She has itching after showers. She does not smoke and takes no medication. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm, BP 146/88 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her GP wants to confirm a suspected raised red cell mass.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A full blood count showing raised haemoglobin and haematocrit is the first step.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Suspected polycythaemia; nothing measured yet.

elim: Not a first-line test.
Done after the blood count confirms a raised haemoglobin.
Interprets a raised haemoglobin once it is found.
May show splenomegaly but does not confirm erythrocytosis.

steps.x: **B. Full blood count with haematocrit.** First-line: FBC (raised Hb and haematocrit).

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has a haemoglobin of 194 g/L (130–180) and haematocrit of 0.57 (0.40–0.52). He has no lung disease and does not smoke. His GP asks which further result would most support polycythaemia vera rather than a secondary cause.
questions.q: Which result would most support polycythaemia vera?
questions.e: In PV, EPO-independent red cell production suppresses EPO; a raised EPO suggests a secondary cause.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
The key separator is the EPO level.

elim: PV usually raises platelets.
PV usually raises white cells.
Points to a secondary cause.
Points to hypoxia and a secondary cause.

steps.x: **B. Low serum erythropoietin.** Low EPO = PV; high EPO = secondary.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has a raised haemoglobin on two blood tests. She is referred to the haematology clinic. The haematologist explains which tests together will confirm whether she has polycythaemia vera and look for another cause.
questions.q: Which is the gold-standard approach to diagnosis?
o: FBC, JAK2, EPO and a search for an underlying cause
questions.e: Polycythaemia is confirmed with FBC, JAK2 mutation, EPO level and assessment of any underlying cause.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.

clues: raised haemoglobin on two blood tests
steps.x: Confirm the clone and exclude secondary causes.

elim: Cannot confirm PV.
Not enough without mutation and EPO testing.
Look only for a secondary cause.
Assess haematinics, not the cause of erythrocytosis.

steps.x: **D. FBC, JAK2, EPO and a search for an underlying cause.** Gold standard: FBC + JAK2 + EPO + look for the cause.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has a haemoglobin of 190 g/L (115–165). Her white cells and platelets are normal, her JAK2 screen is negative and her serum erythropoietin is raised. She does not smoke, her oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air and spirometry is normal. Urinalysis shows blood.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Raised EPO with normal saturation suggests an EPO-producing tumour; haematuria points to the kidney, so image the kidneys.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
Secondary polycythaemia without hypoxia plus haematuria.

elim: JAK2 negative with raised EPO points away from PV.
She is not hypoxic, so a shunt is unlikely.
No snoring or sleepiness and normal saturation.
Will not change; the clues point to a renal source of EPO.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound of the kidneys.** Raised EPO, normal saturation: look for an EPO-secreting tumour.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man with a BMI of 41 kg/m² has a haemoglobin of 191 g/L (130–180) and raised serum erythropoietin. His JAK2 screen is negative. His wife says he snores loudly and stops breathing at night. He falls asleep driving. His oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air while awake.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the cause?
questions.e: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas and sleepiness in obesity suggest obstructive sleep apnoea, a common cause of secondary polycythaemia; confirm with a sleep study.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.

clues: snores loudly and stops breathing at night
steps.x: Secondary polycythaemia with classic OSA symptoms.

elim: PV is unlikely with negative JAK2 and high EPO.
No haematuria or loin symptoms; sleep apnoea is far more likely.
No cyanosis or murmur.
No smoking history or chest symptoms suggesting COPD.

steps.x: **D. Overnight sleep study.** Assess the underlying cause: OSA needs a sleep study.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a haemoglobin of 199 g/L (130–180) with a raised platelet count. His spleen is just palpable. His serum erythropoietin is low. He has no lung or heart disease and his oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most important diagnostic test?
questions.e: JAK2 mutation screening is the most important diagnostic test for polycythaemia vera.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must do here (rule out, confirm, or assess) before reading the options.
High Hb, low EPO, splenomegaly: likely PV.

elim: Can confirm splenomegaly but not the diagnosis.
He is not hypoxic.
For chronic myeloid leukaemia.
Does not confirm PV.

steps.x: **D. JAK2 mutation screen.** Confirm PV with a JAK2 mutation screen.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has polycythaemia vera. He has had three venesections over 6 weeks. He feels well and takes aspirin 75 mg daily. His haematocrit today is 0.48 (0.40–0.52). He has had no thrombosis.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop venesection, as the haematocrit is normal
questions.e: In PV, venesection continues until the haematocrit is kept below 0.45.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Haematocrit is above the PV target.

elim: No indication for anticoagulation.
He is low risk and venesection is working.
Aspirin protects against thrombosis.
The PV target is below 0.45, not just the normal range.

steps.x: **B. Further venesection.** PV: venesect to keep haematocrit <0.45.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man has newly confirmed JAK2-positive polycythaemia vera. His haematocrit is 0.56 (0.40–0.52) and platelets are 480 ×10⁹/L (150–400). He has had no thrombosis or bleeding and has no peptic ulcer history.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: PV first-line: venesection to haematocrit <0.45 plus low-dose aspirin 75 mg once daily (platelets below 1500).

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Low-risk new PV with a high haematocrit.

elim: Does not reduce red cell mass.
Reserved for high-risk or uncontrolled disease.
Leaves him at high risk of thrombosis.
Not used for primary prevention in PV.

steps.x: **D. Venesection and aspirin 75 mg daily.** PV first line: venesection + aspirin 75 mg OD.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with polycythaemia vera has had two DVTs in the past year despite venesection and aspirin. Her haematocrit is often above 0.50 between venesections, and her veins are now difficult to access. Her renal and liver function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: High-risk or uncontrolled PV (older age, recurrent thrombosis) needs cytoreductive therapy with hydroxycarbamide.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: two DVTs in the past year
steps.x: Older, recurrent thrombosis, poorly controlled on venesection.

elim: Treats chronic myeloid leukaemia.
Raises bleeding risk without controlling the disease.
No role in PV.
A second-line option; hydroxycarbamide is first-line cytoreduction.

steps.x: **A. Hydroxycarbamide.** High-risk PV: hydroxycarbamide.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a haemoglobin of 188 g/L (130–180) with a raised serum erythropoietin and a negative JAK2 screen. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day and has moderate COPD. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. He has no thrombosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Secondary polycythaemia is treated by addressing the cause: stop smoking and optimise COPD oxygenation.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
Secondary polycythaemia driven by smoking and COPD.

elim: Treatment for PV, which he does not have.
A JAK inhibitor for myeloproliferative disease.
No role.
The PV target; in secondary polycythaemia treat the cause first.

steps.x: **C. Smoking cessation support.** Secondary polycythaemia: treat the cause (stop smoking, optimise COPD, CPAP for OSA).

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with polycythaemia vera has had 1 hour of weakness of her left arm and face and slurred speech. Her haematocrit last week was 0.55. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and regular, BP 162/90 mmHg and capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
questions.e: Stroke symptoms in polycythaemia are a thrombotic emergency needing urgent assessment, starting with urgent CT head.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.
An acute stroke in a patient with PV.

elim: Delays emergency stroke assessment.
Imaging must exclude haemorrhage before treatment.
Far too slow for an acute stroke.
Not an emergency stroke treatment.

steps.x: **E. Urgent CT head.** Thrombotic complications in polycythaemia need urgent assessment.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has secondary polycythaemia with a haemoglobin of 197 g/L (130–180) and a raised serum erythropoietin. CT shows a 5 cm solid mass in the left kidney with no metastases. He is fit and well otherwise.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Secondary polycythaemia is treated by treating the cause; removing an EPO-producing renal tumour corrects it.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now, given the clues, before reading the options.

clues: solid mass in the left kidney
steps.x: An EPO-secreting renal tumour.

elim: For PV; his problem is an EPO-secreting tumour.
For obstructive sleep apnoea.
Does not treat the tumour driving EPO.
He is not hypoxic.

steps.x: **E. Nephrectomy.** Secondary polycythaemia: treat the cause, including any tumour.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with polycythaemia vera is started on hydroxycarbamide after a stroke. A pharmacist explains that the drug slows DNA synthesis in dividing marrow cells by blocking one enzyme.
questions.q: Which enzyme does hydroxycarbamide inhibit?
questions.e: Hydroxycarbamide inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, reducing DNA synthesis and controlling erythrocytosis.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
The enzyme makes deoxyribonucleotides for DNA.

elim: Blocked by aspirin.
Blocked by methotrexate.
Blocked by ruxolitinib.
Blocked by etoposide and anthracyclines.

steps.x: **D. Ribonucleotide reductase.** Hydroxycarbamide = ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with polycythaemia vera has had regular venesection for 3 years. Her haematocrit stays below 0.45 and she feels well. She asks why she cannot stop treatment if her blood is now normal.
questions.q: Which best explains why venesection does not cure her disease?
o: It does not affect the clonal stem cell
It raises the platelet count to dangerous levels
questions.e: Venesection lowers red cell mass and viscosity, reducing thrombosis risk, but the underlying clonal proliferation continues.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
Treatment controls the red cell mass, not the cause.

elim: Venesection removes iron, it does not add it.
EPO stays suppressed in PV.
Not why it fails to cure.
Venesection does not cause mutations.

steps.x: **B. It does not affect the clonal stem cell.** Venesection reduces viscosity, not the clone.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man with polycythaemia vera has intense itching every time he gets out of a warm bath, lasting about 30 minutes. There is no rash. He asks why the water makes him itch.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Bile salt deposition in the skin
Histamine release from mast cells and basophils
questions.e: Aquagenic pruritus is thought to be due to abnormal histamine release from mast cells and basophils triggered by the temperature change of water contact.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
Water-triggered itch without a rash in PV.

elim: Causes the itch of cholestasis.
Would cause a rash.
Can cause itch but is not triggered by water.
Itch of renal failure, not water-triggered.

steps.x: **C. Histamine release from mast cells and basophils.** Aquagenic pruritus = histamine release from mast cells/basophils.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with severe COPD has an oxygen saturation of 86% breathing air and a haemoglobin of 193 g/L (130–180). His serum erythropoietin is raised. A student asks where the extra erythropoietin comes from.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his raised erythropoietin?
o: Ectopic EPO from a lung tumour
questions.e: In secondary polycythaemia, tissue hypoxia (here from COPD) drives a physiological, compensatory rise in EPO from the kidney.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
Chronic hypoxia from lung disease.

elim: That is PV, where EPO is low.
Rare; chronic hypoxia from COPD is the obvious driver.
Not the mechanism.
No history of steroid use.

steps.x: **D. Renal response to tissue hypoxia.** Secondary: hypoxia or ectopic EPO drives a high EPO.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a haemoglobin of 186 g/L (130–180). His doctor explains he has true (absolute) polycythaemia rather than a raised concentration from low plasma volume, and that his risk of clots is raised.
questions.q: Which finding defines true polycythaemia?
questions.e: Polycythaemia is an abnormally increased red cell mass, raising blood viscosity and thrombosis risk; it may be primary (PV) or secondary.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
True vs relative polycythaemia.

elim: Would dilute, not raise, the haemoglobin.
Can occur in PV but does not define polycythaemia.
Describes red cell size, not mass.
That is pseudopolycythaemia.

steps.x: **B. Increased red cell mass.** Polycythaemia = raised red cell mass (PV or secondary).

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has polycythaemia vera with a JAK2 V617F mutation and low serum erythropoietin. In a laboratory study, her marrow erythroid progenitors are cultured with no erythropoietin added.
questions.q: Which is the most likely result?
o: Colonies grow only at high erythropoietin doses
Red cell colonies grow without erythropoietin
questions.e: In PV, JAK2 V617F makes erythroid progenitors proliferate independently of EPO, which is why serum EPO is appropriately suppressed.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to the underlying mechanism before reading the options.
The clone does not need the normal growth signal.

elim: JAK2 drives myeloid lines, not lineage switching.
That is the normal or hyporesponsive pattern.
Normal progenitors would fail; hers do not.
Constitutive JAK-STAT signalling prevents this.

steps.x: **E. Red cell colonies grow without erythropoietin.** PV: EPO-independent erythropoiesis, so EPO is low.
